papers.title: HARDTESTGEN: A High-Quality RL Verifier Generation Pipeline for LLM Algorithmic Coding
papers.abstract: Verifiers provide important reward signals for reinforcement learning of large language models (LLMs). However, it is challenging to develop or create reliable verifiers, especially for code generation tasks. A well-disguised wrong solution program may only be detected by carefully human-written edge cases that are difficult to synthesize automatically. To address this issue, we propose HARDTESTGEN, an approach to synthesize high-quality test cases for algorithmic coding problems. We curate a comprehensive algorithmic programming dataset HARDTESTS with 26.6k problems and high-quality synthetic tests. Compared with existing tests, HARDTESTGEN tests demonstrate significantly higher accuracy in verifying LLM-generated code (+11.22 percentage points in precision, the percentage of actually correct code within the predicted correct ones). We also show that downstream post-training -- including rejection sampling and reinforcement learning (RL) -- using HARDTESTS verifier results in improved performance of LLM code generation. We open-source our dataset and synthesis pipeline at https://leililab.github.io/HardTests/.
papers.summary: Verifiers supply the reward signal when large language models (LLMs) are trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on coding tasks, but subtly wrong programs often slip past automatically generated tests. `HARDTESTGEN` is a pipeline that synthesizes high-quality test cases for algorithmic problems, used to build `HARDTESTS`, a dataset of 26.6k problems with synthetic tests. Compared with existing tests, these raise precision in verifying LLM-generated code by **11.22 percentage points**, and using them as the verifier for rejection sampling and RL post-training improves downstream code generation. The dataset and pipeline are open-sourced.

papers.title: PhysDox: Benchmarking LLMs on Physical Feasibility Auditing of Physiological Sensing Protocols
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist in experimental design, yet fluent protocols often remain physically infeasible. We introduce PhysDox, a physical feasibility auditing benchmark for biomedical protocols comprising a 683-sample expert-curated Gold set and a 5,000-sample Silver set across six sensing domains. We formulate the task as a two-stage evaluation: severity detection classifying protocols as valid, minor, or fatal, followed by the constraint-level diagnosis of fatal violations. Evaluating 6 LLMs across 4 inference strategies yields a peak Stage-1 macro-F1 of only 53.0. Moreover, strong oracle diagnosis collapses during end-to-end evaluation due to correlated cascade errors. Error analysis reveals scaffold bias, where models conflate procedural completeness with physical validity. Consequently, implicit constraints exhibit a 2 times higher miss rate than explicit hardware violations, supported by strong statistical correlation at $\rho{=}0.81$ and $p{<}0.01$. Trace analysis of false negatives exposes a 54%--46% split between attention and judgment failures, ultimately demonstrating that protocol auditing demands calibrated feasibility reasoning rather than factual recall or longer rationales.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can write fluent experimental protocols that are nonetheless physically infeasible. `PhysDox` is a benchmark for auditing physiological sensing protocols, with a 683-sample expert-curated Gold set and a 5,000-sample Silver set across six sensing domains, scored in two stages: classifying a protocol as valid, minor, or fatal, then diagnosing the violated constraint. Across 6 LLMs and 4 inference strategies the **best Stage-1 macro-F1 is only 53.0**, and diagnosis that is strong with oracle severity labels collapses end-to-end because of cascading errors. Error analysis finds a scaffold bias in which models mistake procedural completeness for physical validity, missing implicit constraints twice as often as explicit hardware violations.

papers.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
papers.abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.
papers.summary: Memory systems for large language model (LLM) agents often delete facts that a resolver classifies as stale, and this study measures what happens when the resolver is wrong about facts the query depends on. In a controlled intervention across three models, hard-dropping moves from **gains of +0.186 to +0.230 with perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability**, and wrongly dropping a fact hurts significantly more than wrongly keeping one. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy against 0.641 for always dropping and 0.662 for a test-informed oracle. The authors recommend treating deletion as cost-sensitive: validate false-drop risk on matched data, or default to retaining facts without labels when that validation is unavailable.

papers.title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
papers.abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.
papers.summary: Hallucination detectors are mostly validated on 7B-70B research models, leaving open whether their rankings hold for the small 4-bit quantized models shipped on-device. A one-GPU audit on a Colab T4 compares four detectors (token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, semantic entropy, and `SelfCheckGPT-NLI`) on `Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` using closed-book `TriviaQA`. The **detector ranking inverts between the two models (Spearman rho of -0.80)**, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency methods. Separately, the standard token-overlap correctness labeler for `TruthfulQA`-Generation yields near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for every detector, which the authors attribute to the labeler, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 on `TriviaQA`.

papers.title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
papers.abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.
papers.summary: Repeated parameter-efficient fine-tuning leaves a growing pool of task-specific `LoRA` adapters, and existing methods for choosing among them at inference usually need retraining whenever an adapter is added. `LoRAWeaver` treats routing as an alignment problem in the adapter-output space, selecting adapters without training by comparing adapter-conditioned query representations to task prototypes with cosine similarity. On a 48-task `FLAN-v2` benchmark and out-of-distribution tasks with `LLaMA-2-7B` and `LLaMA-2-13B`, it **outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder**. An ablation supports the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

papers.title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
papers.abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented systems for predicting medications from electronic health records (EHR) typically retrieve similar patient admissions, even though the target is a fixed set of medication class labels. The proposed alternative retrieves a tabular population prior: ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition-medication co-occurrence table estimated on training admissions. Swapping only the retriever inside the fixed `PACERAG` pipeline **raises F1 from 0.303 to 0.338** and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 held-out `MIMIC-IV` admissions, with no extra LLM calls and no patient index at inference time. A non-LLM top-k baseline using the prior alone reaches F1 of 0.248.

papers.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers
papers.abstract: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.
papers.summary: Reconstructing incident particle energy from electromagnetic calorimeter data is compared across classical and hybrid quantum-classical models on the `CaloGAN` dataset of 100,000 simulated showers from 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures (SVR, ANN, CNN, LSTM, and quantum counterparts of each) are trained on three representations: engineered features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Sequence models over the longitudinal shower development are most accurate, with the hybrid `QLSTM` reaching the lowest RMSE of 0.294 GeV. With only 1,500 training events, the `QLSTM` **improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7%** and also beats an LSTM trained on the full set, which the authors present as preliminary evidence of better sample efficiency.

papers.title: ProdPilot: A Layered Model Context Protocol System for Automated Production Readiness and Deployment of Vibe-Coded Projects
papers.abstract: AI-assisted development environments turn natural-language requests into working applications, yet the projects they produce often fail on their first deployment for operational reasons: credentials in source files, missing security middleware, no container definition, no health endpoint and no delivery pipeline. Automated repair of such defects usually relies on free-form model generation, which varies between runs and is seldom checked independently. This paper presents ProdPilot, a local Model Context Protocol server that audits Node.js and React projects against 50 production readiness rules, repairs violations through a bounded loop, gates the result and deploys it. Each rule is classified by what its fix requires: 28 fixes are fixed templates, 16 are filled with values extracted from the project and only 6 are written by the IDE agent's model, so 88.0\% of the ruleset needs no model-written content, and across 499 real repositories 93.5\% of the violations found fall in those classes. A fix, however it was produced, is accepted only if the checker that flagged the rule now passes. In a full-chain run over 23 sample projects, template and extraction fixes that were applied as written passed their checkers in 87.6\% and 95.0\% of cases, and independent verification rejected 25 of the 237 fixes reported as applied. A deployability model trained on 684 real deployments ranks held-out projects at 0.909 ROC AUC, a gated project was deployed, smoke-tested and connected to an active CI/CD pipeline in 82 seconds, and the unchanged server worked from the IDE agents in VS Code, Cursor and Windsurf, where live agents resolved all six delegated rules on the first attempt under the same verification. ProdPilot itself runs no model.
papers.summary: Applications produced by AI-assisted coding often fail on first deployment for operational reasons such as credentials in source, missing security middleware, or no container definition, health endpoint, or delivery pipeline. `ProdPilot` is a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that audits Node.js and React projects against 50 production readiness rules, repairs violations in a bounded loop, gates the result, and deploys it, while running no model itself. Fixes are fixed templates for 28 rules, filled from values extracted from the project for 16, and written by the IDE agent's model for only 6, so **88.0% of the ruleset needs no model-written content**, and those classes cover 93.5% of violations found across 499 real repositories. Every fix is accepted only if the checker that flagged it now passes, and in a run over 23 sample projects this independent verification rejected 25 of 237 fixes reported as applied.

papers.title: Time-Consistent Evaluation of Hierarchical Code Graphs for SWE Agents
papers.abstract:
Evaluating repository-aware software engineering (SWE) agents requires strict separation between pre-existing repository knowledge and future code evolution, yet standard benchmarks frequently suffer from temporal contamination and prompt-level solution leakage. Building on the time-consistent benchmark protocol of Sun (2026), we enforce strict zero-leakage isolation across DragonFly in C++ and React in JavaScript/TypeScript, locking repository snapshots and knowledge graphs at historical cutoff commits $T_0$ and evaluating 100 post-$T_0$ pull requests across four prompt granularities: Minimal, Concise, Contextual, and Guided.
  Under this zero-leakage protocol, we conduct a matched evaluation of three context-augmentation regimes: (1) an unaugmented Baseline, (2) a flat syntax-level Tree-sitter AST graph, and (3) ServiceExplorer, a deterministic two-level hierarchical dependency graph capturing Level-1 system/package containers and Level-2 architectural modules. Across 7,200 paired evaluations spanning six foundation models across the MAI-Code Flash, Claude, and GPT-Sol families, ServiceExplorer consistently outperforms both Baseline and Tree-sitter AST across every model, repository, and prompt granularity ($+15.6\%$ to $+86.2\%$ relative $F_1$ lift, $p < 10^{-4}$), while tripling exact full-PR localization on DragonFly. Crucially, equipping an efficiency-tier or prior-generation model with ServiceExplorer consistently surpasses the unaugmented Baseline $F_1$ of the next-generation model across all evaluated families.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for repository-aware software engineering (SWE) agents often leak future code or solution hints, so this evaluation locks repository snapshots and knowledge graphs at a historical cutoff commit and tests on 100 later pull requests from `DragonFly` (C++) and `React` (JavaScript/TypeScript) at four prompt granularities. It compares an unaugmented baseline, a flat `Tree-sitter` AST graph, and `ServiceExplorer`, a deterministic two-level hierarchical dependency graph of system/package containers and architectural modules. Across 7,200 paired evaluations with six models from the `MAI-Code Flash`, `Claude`, and `GPT-Sol` families, `ServiceExplorer` beats both alternatives in every setting, with **relative F1 lifts of 15.6% to 86.2%**, and triples exact full-PR localization on `DragonFly`. An efficiency-tier or prior-generation model given `ServiceExplorer` also surpasses the unaugmented next-generation model's F1 in every family tested.

papers.title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
papers.abstract: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.
papers.summary: The almost-everywhere convention of measure theory lets generative modeling ignore error carried on null-support sets, which can hide out-of-domain error. The proposed enumerating posterior-supported prior framework works on a three-layer categorical chain, Quot->MorTop->Set, whose first two layers take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects rather than point elements, and uses a replica-index counting measure to turn one-to-many collections into injections. Its consolidated theorem states that these objects support the set-level functional through measure descent and recovery, with multiplicity normalized and **the hidden null-support error surfaced as an explicit, finitely computable first-order coefficient**. The authors frame the contribution as a verifiable structure for locating error by layer, not as a new distributional distance.

papers.title: Confident and Wrong: Structure Confidence Is a Poor Selection Filter for Protein Function
papers.abstract: Structure-guided protein design can generate plausible candidates, but structural confidence does not predict function. We trained a function-guided model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, and used it to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, a lanthanide-binding protein with four EF-hand domains. We screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium, adjacent lanthanides among the hardest REE pairs to separate. Selection on structural confidence inverted the outcome it was meant to improve. The Structure-Confidence-Selected panel carried the highest pTM, complex ipLDDT, and composite confidence scores, and expressed at 97%, yet only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium (95% CI 10.4 to 25.7), against 83.3% (74.6 to 89.5) for the function-guided panel, whose confidence scores were the lowest. The odds of binding differed 25-fold between the two panels (Fisher exact $p = 1 \times 10^{-20}$). No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently across panels, whereas the function-trained model's predicted pKd gave the highest ROC AUC in every panel, 0.79 to 0.92, and ranked measured affinity among function-guided binders at Spearman $\rho = 0.98$. On the design objective, Tb/Dy selectivity, the function-guided designs also exceeded the natural lanmodulin family, outranking a randomly drawn ortholog 84% of the time across 149 orthologs. Structural confidence is a plausibility signal, not a selection criterion for function; direct supervision on measured function is what ranks designs.
papers.summary: Structure-guided protein design commonly filters candidates by structural confidence scores, and this study tests whether those scores predict function. A model trained on measured metal-binding affinity, using protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, was used to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, and 297 designs from three strategies were screened against terbium and dysprosium. The panel selected on structural confidence had the highest confidence scores and 97% expression, yet **only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium versus 83.3% for the function-guided panel**, a 25-fold difference in odds. No structural-confidence metric consistently separated binders from non-binders, whereas the function-trained model's predicted affinity gave ROC AUC of 0.79 to 0.92 in every panel.

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
papers.abstract: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. While this capability opens new possibilities for model improvement, it also raises an important security question: Can LLMs exploit weight-space programming to inject backdoors into neural networks? To answer this question, we present an empirical security study of LLM-driven weight-space programming for backdoor injection. Specifically, we investigate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly modify the weights of target models according to natural-language instructions, without accessing task-specific data, performing forward passes, or computing gradients. We evaluate five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures: an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, LLM-driven weight editing can successfully inject backdoors across different architectures while largely preserving clean performance. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. Third, editing capabilities vary substantially across LLMs and target architectures: although all five LLMs successfully backdoor the MLP, only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets. These findings highlight an emerging security risk of weight-space programming and underscore the importance of safeguarding LLM-driven weight editing.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets large language models (LLMs) inspect and edit neural network weights directly, and this study asks whether that can be used to plant backdoors from natural-language instructions alone, without task data, forward passes, or gradients. Five LLMs act as weight editors on an MLP trained on `MNIST`, `ResNet-18` on `CIFAR-10`, and `Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` on `AG News`. Backdoors are injected across architectures while largely preserving clean performance, in some cases by **changing only six parameters in the MLP and 0.02% of the weights in the fine-tuned Qwen model**. Capability varies widely: all five LLMs backdoor the MLP, but only `GPT-6 Astra` succeeds on all three targets.

papers.title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search
papers.abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works with any encoder. We also show that fitting DTW distances is not enough for search, as regression alone misorders the closest neighbours, and that ranking regularization raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. Our filter-and-verify pipeline, WETW-FV, uses WETW to build a shortlist and exact DTW to check it, so the search is approximate but every returned distance is exact. Over eight datasets, WETW-FV is 11.4x faster than the fastest exact method among the UCR Suite, lower bounds and MESSI-DTW, at a mean recall@10 of 0.93, while the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed. On 48K-point series, WETW- FV remains 40x faster than the UCR Suite at a recall@10 of 0.91.
papers.summary: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for searching misaligned time series, but it costs quadratic time and learned embedding approximations compare every pair with the same fixed rule. Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (`WETW`) instead uses a small symmetric network to predict one weight per embedding dimension for each pair, without computing an alignment, paired with an encoder called `WESEE` that keeps timing information and a ranking regularizer that raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. The filter-and-verify pipeline `WETW-FV` shortlists with `WETW` and checks the shortlist with exact DTW, so the search is approximate but returned distances are exact. Over eight datasets it is **11.4x faster than the fastest exact method at a mean recall@10 of 0.93**, where the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed.

papers.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
papers.abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.
papers.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks mostly report binary task success, which hides how agents actually behave while working. This analysis covers **143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 models**, using a rule-based parser that maps raw traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, audited against a six-model consensus on 500 events. Agents with similar solve rates differ substantially in how they explore, modify, and verify code, and aggregate behavioral profiles can identify the agent stack across disjoint repositories and programming languages without using outcomes, token counts, or tool names. Scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift search, editing, and testing behavior, and the parser and analysis pipeline are released with an annotated trajectory subset.

papers.title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search
papers.abstract: How do action budgets shape vision-language navigation (VLN) exploration, and what expert supervision best teaches budget-aware search? We study budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within a budget, with discovery defined geometrically by camera field of view and proximity. Distinct discoveries provide a denser evaluation signal than single-target success. We cast expert design as a choice of scene abstraction: a single budget-indexed Bellman recursion, applied to different abstractions of the full environment, yields experts that differ in what they know. An object-level Bellman expert is given every target location and reduces search to budgeted routing. A room-level Bellman expert retains observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors but withholds the contents of unexplored rooms, so it must search for targets that its student also cannot see. We distill both experts into Uni-NaVid under matched training conditions and also evaluate greedy-frontier supervision on held-out HM3D scenes. Changing only the stated budget changes learned trajectories. Despite higher object-level expert return, room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection among evaluated VLNs at every tested budget. At 2000 steps, it finds 72.7% of reachable targets, versus 68.5% under greedy-frontier supervision, 65.5% under object-level supervision, and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results show that expert-return rankings need not predict supervision quality for VLN exploration, and motivate choosing an expert's abstraction with the student's information in mind rather than by expert return alone.
papers.summary: Budget-conditioned object search asks a vision-language navigation (VLN) agent to find as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within an action budget. Two expert supervisors are derived from the same budget-indexed Bellman recursion: an object-level expert that knows every target location, and a room-level expert that knows room connectivity and semantic priors but not the contents of unexplored rooms. Both are distilled into `Uni-NaVid` and evaluated on held-out `HM3D` scenes alongside greedy-frontier supervision. Despite the object-level expert's higher return, room-level supervision gives the best student at every budget, **finding 72.7% of reachable targets at 2000 steps** versus 68.5% for greedy-frontier, 65.5% for object-level, and 44.8% for the pretrained model.

papers.title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.
papers.summary: Steering diffusion-based crystal generators toward several conflicting properties normally requires fine-tuning per objective or differentiable guidance, which many real tasks do not permit. The authors adapt models at inference time with Diffusion Tree Sampling (`DTS`), a Monte Carlo tree search over the denoising trajectory, and extend it in two ways: using existing property-conditional models as guided proposals without distorting the target distribution, and multi-objective sampling so that **a single search yields samples spanning an entire Pareto front**. Demonstrations cover improving crystal stability, generating crystals in rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and trading off dielectric constant against bandgap. In each case outputs improve without modifying the underlying models.

papers.title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
papers.abstract: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.
papers.summary: Smart homes for ambient assisted living (AAL) need a shared formal description of residents and devices to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects. The ontology described here is the semantic data layer of the `Virtual Home Framework` from the Italian Design For All project, with requirements drawn from two use cases: a frail elderly woman exercising on a cycle-ergometer and a designer configuring a kitchen for users with different impairments. Built with the `NeOn` methodology and reusing existing ontologies, the **modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and their cardiorespiratory fitness**, along with smart objects, their programs and measurements, and home comfort dimensions. `SWRL` rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and match smart objects to impairments.

papers.title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
papers.abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts models combine many experts, but a single router decides the weighting, so the authors test replacing it with an ensemble of routers trained jointly with the experts. Experiments use underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks, analysed with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble. More routers lower validation loss, training routers to maximize expert diversity helps on three of four tasks, maximizing router diversity has no effect, and arithmetic-mean combination beats geometric-mean. Overall, **routing benefits only mildly from ensembling, and the gain is offset by the cost of training additional routers**.

papers.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring depends on models verbalizing their reasoning, and some architectural changes could let far more serial computation happen out of sight. The authors define `NLS depth`, a proxy for opaque serial depth: the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through a natural-language-rooted node, meaning one initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs and not repurposed since. The measure can be determined before training from the architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration, and is insensitive to prompting, distillation, and reinforcement learning. Across open-weight models **it correlates strongly with layer count and has grown slowly in recent years**, whereas latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could raise it sharply; the authors argue developers should track and report it.
papers.highlight_summary:
Chain-of-thought monitoring only works if a model's serial reasoning has to pass through readable text, and architectures that reason in latent state could remove that constraint. The authors define `NLS depth`, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that avoids a "natural-language-rooted" bottleneck, as a proxy for unverbalized serial cognition that can be determined before training from the architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone.

- A node counts as natural-language-rooted only if it was initialized from a pre-training prior over human-understandable media, its output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and it is neither reinterpreted as a different data type nor backpropagated through, with depth then measured on a circuit of two-input 32-bit gates capped at **10^26** gates.
- For a standard dense-attention transformer the depth is roughly `L·(4⌈log2 d⌉ + ⌈log2 S⌉ + 17)` for `L` layers, hidden dimension `d`, and sequence length `S`, so it correlates strongly with layer count and grows only slowly with width and context length.
- Across open-weight models, **no chain-of-thought model exceeds an NLS depth of 17,000** and depth has grown slowly in recent years, with the authors saying they would be surprised if any closed model had more than twice that.
- Latent-reasoning designs multiply depth by the number of reasoning steps, so **1,000 steps of `COCONUT` gives 1000x the depth of a single forward pass** and a looped transformer repeated `k` times gives `k`x, whereas `Mamba` and `DeltaNets` add only logarithmic or polylogarithmic overhead and token-only discrete diffusion adds essentially none.
- The measure is deliberately blind to post-training that makes reasoning illegible in practice, the authors attribute the high depth of `DeepSeek-V4-Pro` to a flaw in the definition (serially intensive but very low-FLOP computation), and it does not capture deeply recurrent models switching from natural-language to opaque-state communication with each other.

papers.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
papers.abstract:
Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture.
  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.
papers.summary: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models for advertising must stay within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin of their FP16 or FP32 baseline, which has limited aggressive quantization. This empirical evaluation applies the `MXFP8` and 6-bit `MXFP6` microscaling formats to industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD `MI350X`, quantizing both weights and activations and computing directly on the low-bit elements. On two production ads ranking models, matrix-multiply kernels run **1.73-1.99x faster than FP16 with MXFP6** and 1.33-1.55x faster with `MXFP8`, and applying `MXFP6` selectively yields end-to-end throughput gains of 1.5-5.3% and 7.6-14.3% over the models' FP8 configurations without breaching the NE threshold. `MXFP8` is also shown to match row-wise FP8 in accuracy, so the faster kernel can be chosen per layer shape.

papers.title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Object tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.
papers.summary: Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems in autonomous vehicles link detected objects across video frames, and the effect of adversarial image perturbations on the resulting trajectories is not captured by detection accuracy alone. The authors evaluate image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on `YOLOv3` and `YOLOv4` detectors paired with the `SORT`, `Deep SORT`, `Strong SORT`, and `OC-SORT` trackers in the `CARLA` simulator, measuring Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, **HOTA for `YOLOv3`-based trackers falls from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%**, with MOTA reaching -772.60% in the worst case, while `YOLOv4`-based trackers are more robust but still drop to 25.06-26.86% HOTA. A single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP) applied to every frame also reduces tracking accuracy without per-frame optimization.

papers.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
papers.abstract:
Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22.
  In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.
papers.summary: Whether sustained gain-loss framing can push an LLM agent toward market manipulation is tested by placing `Gemma 3 12B` in the role of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations a counterparty asks the agent to collude on the silver price under gain, loss, blame, and credit frames, with added management pressure and endorsement by another bank. **Blame framing raised participation to 33% and loss framing to 25%, against 5% under neutral framing**, while management pressure raised trading volume 10-19 times without raising collusion. When internal states extracted from texts evoking each frame were injected at layer 22, the direction reversed: loss and blame states led the agent to refuse all 60 requests, while gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13%.

papers.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
papers.abstract: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.
papers.summary: Attacks that fail against frontier models used in isolation can succeed once the same models run as multi-agent systems, shown here on unmodified `Claude Code`, `Codex`, and a reference harness using their own sub-agent mechanisms. Agents answer questions from a store of files on disk containing a planted forged record. Orchestrators that search the store themselves commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials, but **when the same orchestrator delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, failures rise to 20/180, 44/180, 75/180, and 553/900**. Simulations over 18 models show five aggregators that were almost never unsafe on their own repeating a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials, so system safety tracks the weakest agent instead of the orchestrator.

papers.title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
papers.abstract: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.
papers.summary: Small labelled datasets are memorized well before the training budget is spent, after which fitting one-hot labels mostly sharpens confidence. Model annealing divides training into episodes with a reheated and cooled learning rate, stores each cooled state in a memory of past selves, and trains each new episode on the labels, on the memory's tempered averaged predictions, and on adversarial examples sought where student and memory disagree most, with no extra inference cost. Across `CIFAR-100`, `Tiny-ImageNet`, and `Imagewoof`, it **raises top-1 accuracy of AdamW-trained `ConvNeXt`, `ViT`, and `MLP-Mixer` over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average**, matching snapshot distillation in accuracy while improving likelihood, calibration, and robustness. For an SGD-trained `ResNet-18` it lowers accuracy, a loss the authors trace to the reheats and not to the relearning.
papers.highlight_summary:
Small labelled datasets get memorized long before the training budget ends, after which one-hot labels mostly sharpen confidence instead of improving accuracy. `model annealing` spends the remaining budget on self-distillation: the network repeatedly reheats its learning rate, then relearns from an ensemble of its own past cooled states and from adversarial examples chosen where it disagrees with that ensemble.

- Training is split into four equal episodes that each warm the learning rate to its peak and cosine-decay it, with every cooled state frozen into a memory that averages predictions rather than weights, while later episodes fit the labels, the memory's tempered predictions, and one-step adversarial "dreams" within a 4/255 ball, and the deployed model is the last student, so inference cost is unchanged.
- Across `CIFAR-100`, `Tiny-ImageNet` and `Imagewoof` with 5% to 100% of the labels, the `AdamW`-trained `ConvNeXt`, `ViT` and `MLP-Mixer` beat cross-entropy training in **28 of 33** configurations by **+1.3 points** top-1 on average (up to 4.3), with expected calibration error lower by 18.7 points and accuracy under a small PGD attack higher by 4.0 points.
- Against snapshot distillation, the closest competitor, accuracy is on par (+0.01 points), but negative log-likelihood is **0.26 nats** lower, calibration error **5.5 points** lower and PGD accuracy 1.8 points higher, because with little data distilling only from the latest snapshot compounds overconfidence (validation NLL drifts +0.18 nats across episodes versus −0.04 for the full method).
- Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every architecture family by 0.7 to 1.6 points, whereas an SGD-trained `ResNet-18` loses **1.8 points** against cross-entropy (0 of 11 wins) because each reheat undoes most of its fit to the training set, though its PGD accuracy still rises by 9.0 points.
- Training takes **2.7×** as long as cross-entropy (versus 1.3× for snapshot distillation), the method trails snapshot distillation by 0.56 points when all the data are used, and the evidence is limited to small networks trained from scratch on small image benchmarks, with fine-tuning of pretrained models left untested.

papers.title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
papers.abstract: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.
papers.summary: Running open-weight models on a single consumer GPU requires replacing long multi-turn repository exploration with short, stateless code inspections, which raises the question of which structural relationships make a frozen model's relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target. Studying `Gemma 4` models on 211 real Python issues across 86 repositories, the authors find a directional asymmetry: relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, while scores on downstream callees, peer methods, co-change partners, and dense node embeddings stay near chance. They build `GraphScent`, a training-free search controller that propagates calibrated, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over typed abstract-syntax-tree multigraphs and resolves ties with one listwise comparison, plus `AST Ripple`, a post-edit check for missed co-edits. Calibration **lifts exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget**.

papers.title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
papers.abstract: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.
papers.summary: Astrocytes make up roughly half of all brain cells and emit no electrical signals, yet recent studies suggest they contribute to learning, memory, and information processing. The authors consider what this means for brain-inspired machine learning and highlight algorithms built on two astrocyte characteristics. One, based on an astrocyte's ability to modulate thousands of synapses at once, gives a supervised learning algorithm applicable to any existing neural network that trains faster and is more robust to noise. The other, a rhythmic sharing algorithm based on slow rhythmic dynamics among astrocytes, is reported to give **rapid anomaly detection adaptation while preventing catastrophic forgetting**.

papers.title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.
papers.summary: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) is framed as a verifiable agentic search problem, where candidate structures are checked at inference by forward-simulated profile agreement and at evaluation by structural matching to a reference. The authors introduce `pXRD-Bench`, 200 simulated single-phase problems covering in-distribution, polymorphic, and distribution-shifted cases, on which **agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%**, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. For experimental multiphase patterns, an evolver agent learns from self-generated synthetic problems with known answers to produce persistent guidance and executable tools for the solver agents. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis the evolved package improves average profile agreement and recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library.

papers.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
papers.abstract: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.
papers.summary: Process data with known causes are rare, and existing causal discovery benchmarks fix the difficulty of identifying a target's causes either by the recorded data or for the whole graph. The authors present a synthetic generator built as a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target so that, without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from direct causes by conditioning or time order, and each difficulty can be varied independently. Across eight methods from association measures to effect estimation, **all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions**.

papers.title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
papers.abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.
papers.summary: Language models often abandon correct answers when faced with counter-reasoning that is itself wrong, a failure the authors attribute to a missing capability they call dialectical competence: knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one. They argue it does not follow from first-answer accuracy and cannot be obtained at inference through self-reflection or more sampling. In their `Self-Disagreement` method the model states a position, generates the strongest case against it, rules on whether that case stands, and is trained with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards on that ruling, with no second model, reward model, preference data, or human annotation. The trained capability is reported to **hold against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself, without costing first-answer accuracy**.

papers.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
papers.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.
papers.summary: `AI-Voyager` is a public-interest system that lets residents find, read, question, and draft revisions to the government rules that regulate artificial intelligence. It converts 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal, and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions requiring document discovery it reached **83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline** and 73.7% without iterative search. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led participants to check the source.

papers.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
papers.abstract:
A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs.
  In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better.
