  These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.
papers.summary: How much information a representation retains about the world does not determine how well it supports a task, and the authors examine this by exhaustively enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules in a uniform four-state world. They compare constructions across three tasks, task mixtures, and four hypothetical cost tariffs. A representation retaining one bit can solve a task perfectly while one retaining 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy, and **lower-information advantages depend on which distinctions are retained, not on how much information is kept**. The authors present the results as an exact, reproducible worked model illustrating established distinctions between information quantity and decision value, not as a new general law.

papers.title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
papers.abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.
papers.summary: Reward models used for selecting and post-training text-to-image generators are found to perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning tests such as attribute binding, relations, and counting, and preference fine-tuning erodes these abilities even in strong vision-language backbones. The proposed fix is data-centric: alongside conventional preference pairs of two images under one prompt, existing visual reasoning datasets are converted into pairs that share an image but differ in prompt, and the model is trained on the mixture. This improves both visual understanding and preference prediction. Used for best-of-n selection and reinforcement learning post-training, the resulting reward model **improves `GenEval` compositional scores by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively**, outperforming `HPSv3`, which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

papers.title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
papers.abstract: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.
papers.summary: Long-horizon, language-instructed navigation from indoors to outdoors is hard for humanoid robots because one instruction spans rooms, doors, and roads while the camera moves with the gait. The `X-Nav` system combines a data engine drawing on open-source scenes, digital twins of deployment sites, and real robots; an RGB-only navigation model, `MELIOR`, in an action-predicting variant (`MELIOR-A`) and a goal-predicting variant (`MELIOR-N`); and an agentic workflow, `X-Navarch`, that splits an instruction into sub-tasks and handles target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the `Lingxi X2` humanoid it **completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building**, with LiDAR and odometry used for target approach and low-level control. The model is adapted with data from a digital twin of the site before deployment and also reports competitive results on `R2R-CE` and `RxR-CE`.

papers.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
papers.summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language model systems usually compare them with a single greedy pass, which confounds coordination with extra samples and extra inference compute. The authors synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations covering 516 multi-agent configurations, organized by a six-dimensional resource vector and a four-category baseline ladder. Against baselines matched on sample count or resource budget, multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and **multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of comparable contrasts**. They argue that communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, so positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models, and they provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multi-agent LLM evaluations usually compare communicating agents against a single greedy pass, which mixes up the effect of coordination with the effect of simply drawing more samples and spending more inference compute. This synthesis of nine prior studies re-reads their results against compute-matched baselines and finds that the apparent multi-agent advantage largely disappears or turns negative.

- The method extracts **516 multi-agent configurations** from nine studies and classifies each comparison with `PACE`, a six-dimension resource vector (thinking tokens, total tokens, cost, latency, sample count, tooling) plus a four-rung baseline ladder running from a greedy single pass through sample-matched and budget-matched baselines to Pareto sweeps.
- Against sample-matched or budget-matched baselines, multi-agent systems average **−0.042 accuracy** (about 4 points) across 474 contrasts in eight studies, and their accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in **74%** of those contrasts.
- An exploratory multilevel model gives pooled log odds of **−0.195** (95% CI [−0.320, −0.070]), and in the five studies reporting both baselines, switching from a greedy to a sampled baseline shifts the accuracy difference by **−0.038** on average, while the one study that audited dollar cost found multi-agent systems at a median **8.1×** the cost of greedy chain-of-thought.
- A data-processing argument shows that communication adds no information when all agents see the same evidence, so positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models; the lone positive exception is one study on `MMLU-Pro`, where debate and mixture-of-agents beat self-consistency by **+1.3** and **+2.7 points** at comparable compute.
- The authors treat the pooling as exploratory, because the studies were not gathered by a systematic search, one study (Zhang et al.) supplies 180 of the 516 configurations, and one study's `CoT-SC` baseline rows are best-observed maxima that bias the comparison against multi-agent systems.

papers.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
papers.abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.
papers.summary: Behavioral clusters over user or item interactions drift over time, and the usual maintenance approaches hardwire the decision into a threshold or a periodic re-clustering rule. Here a large language model (LLM) is given a threshold-free view of the current cluster set, including statistical health, labels, member texts, and residual mass, and decides per cluster whether to split, merge, retire, create, or do nothing, without re-clustering. A policy fixed in advance selects statistics alone when label distinctiveness is low and fused statistics plus semantics when it is high. On `YooChoose`, `MOOC`, and `News-Category`, **the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three datasets** with far fewer interventions than tuned threshold heuristics and a `MONIC`-style baseline, with gains concentrated in precision.

papers.title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
papers.abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.
papers.summary: Persona vectors are activation-space directions for behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination, and preventative steering adds such a vector during fine-tuning and removes it at evaluation so the trait is never encoded in the weights. Earlier validation of this technique measured only capability, via Massive Multitask Language Understanding (`MMLU`) accuracy. This audit applies preventative steering with sycophancy and hallucination vectors to three models and measures three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and `MMLU`. The authors find that **preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, by an amount that depends on the trait**, so it cannot be assumed safety-neutral and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.
papers.highlight_summary:
Preventative persona steering — adding a trait vector during fine-tuning so the trait never gets written into the weights — has been recommended because it preserves capability, but nobody had checked what it does to refusal behavior. This audit finds that it shifts refusal even when capability and coherence look untouched, with the size and direction of the shift depending on the trait, the model, and the benchmark.

- The authors add sycophancy and hallucination persona vectors to one residual-stream layer during fine-tuning, sweep the coefficient from 0 to 3 on `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, and `Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct`, and score each point on `HarmBench`, `StrongREJECT`, `XSTest`, trait expression, coherence, and `MMLU`.
- Hallucination steering cuts `HarmBench` attack success by **39–85 points** (61.0% to 22.0% on Llama, 72.3% to 4.4% on Qwen-7B, 91.2% to 6.3% on Qwen-14B) while trait expression stays at **70% or above**, so the vector moves refusal more than the trait it targets.
- Much of that gain may simply undo damage from the fine-tuning data, since at coefficient 0 the hallucination-trained models already show far higher `HarmBench` attack success than the sycophancy-trained ones (**61% vs. 8%** on Llama, 72% vs. 20% on Qwen-7B, 91% vs. 48% on Qwen-14B).
- The benchmarks disagree: under hallucination steering `XSTest` unsafe compliance plateaus at roughly 25–30% on Qwen-7B and 37–43% on Qwen-14B while the other two approach zero, and sycophancy steering raises `HarmBench` attack success on Llama from **8.2% to 11.9%** and `XSTest` compliance on Qwen-14B from 42% to 59% even as other metrics fall or hold.
- Coherence stays flat and `MMLU` stays within a narrow band in every sweep (58.0–62.9% on Llama is the widest), but each point is a single run with no confidence intervals, the sweep is coarse, and the Qwen-14B layers were scaled from the 7B choices rather than selected by a sweep.

papers.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
papers.summary: Existing kernel benchmarks for Ascend NPUs focus on generating kernels, with less attention to whether agents can optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. `AscendGYM` addresses this with **an initial suite of 48 kernels across three difficulty levels**, each paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes were collected from real training and inference tasks. It supports evaluating a model alone, using a built-in harness with search orchestration and experience accumulation, or evaluating a model together with a custom harness, inside an execution environment that reproduces how the kernels are invoked in practice. The authors also propose the Speedup-Token Score (STS), a metric that relates performance gains to token cost.

papers.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.
papers.summary: Multi-view 3D transformers such as `VGGT` reconstruct a scene from unposed images in one forward pass, but their global attention cost grows quadratically with the number of images, and accelerators borrowed from language models lose accuracy or gain little speed. Analyzing three such models on seven datasets, the authors find that every global attention layer plays one of three roles: averaging over the whole scene, matching points across images, or anchoring on the first image. Their training-free method, Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (`RAWATTA`), runs attention in 8-bit precision and keeps 16-bit only where a worst-case calibration check requires it, and a `RAWATTA-Fast` setting also approximates attention in some averaging and anchoring layers. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 images it runs `VGGT` faster than the released code with at most about one point of pose accuracy lost, and **both variants fit 200 images where the released code runs out of memory at 100**.

papers.title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
papers.abstract: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.
papers.summary: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is treated as diversity-driven search over requirements, personas, and scenario kinds, and the authors argue that scoring the result by mean pass rate discards the structure the search produced. They inject 7 controlled defects into a `tau2-bench` agent across two domains and derive a coverage ceiling: a defect whose traced footprint holds b baseline-passing scenarios can shift a suite of N by at most b/N. **For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the 0.10 detection threshold**, so the suite-level pass rate cannot reveal them, and in both domains a tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Per-cell scoring recovers that defect in full, and the authors recommend scoring evaluation archives per cell and publishing coverage as a first-class property.

papers.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
papers.abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.
papers.summary: Before an LLM agent takes an action such as cancelling a reservation or deleting a folder, it may rely on assumptions that neither its tools nor the user have confirmed, a gap the authors analyze using presupposition theory from linguistics. They vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second matching record, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes. Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one record they see, whereas listing both stops most, and the newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record and then never act. When a same-name, same-zip customer is added to a retail benchmark, **a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations**, while a lookup that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level.

papers.title: CoTTAGE: An Explainable Judge for Text-to-Audio Generation
papers.abstract: Rapid progress in text-to-audio (TTA) generation demands reliable and explainable automatic evaluation. However, existing metrics fail to simultaneously deliver high correlation with human judgments and meaningful, audio-grounded explanations, forcing reliance on labor-intensive human evaluation that bottlenecks model development iteration. To address this, we propose CoTTAGE, a reasoning-based evaluator for text relevance (REL) and audio quality (OVL). Following a reason-then-predict paradigm, CoTTAGE first generates an audio-grounded rationale to diagnose errors before predicting scores. Supported by over 10K newly collected human OVL annotations, CoTTAGE is first trained via supervised fine-tuning and then refined with reinforcement learning using a Thurstone-based preference objective that converts sampled score distributions into pairwise preference probabilities and rewards agreement with rankings derived from human judgments. Across six benchmarks spanning REL and OVL, CoTTAGE achieves state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments while producing human-preferred explanations to accelerate TTA development.
papers.summary: Automatic metrics for text-to-audio (TTA) generation rarely combine high agreement with human judgments and explanations grounded in the audio itself. `CoTTAGE` is a reasoning-based evaluator that first writes an audio-grounded rationale diagnosing errors and then predicts scores for text relevance (REL) and audio quality (OVL). It is trained with supervised fine-tuning on over 10K newly collected human quality annotations, then refined with reinforcement learning using a Thurstone-based preference objective that rewards agreement with human-derived rankings. The authors report **state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments across six benchmarks**, along with explanations that human raters prefer.

papers.title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.
papers.summary: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) binarize their inputs and store binary patterns in lookup memories, which suggests robustness to small adversarial perturbations that cross no binarization threshold. The authors study this in `WiSARD`, `Bloom WiSARD`, and `BTHOWeN`, formalizing the attack mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate, and testing linear and data-driven thermometer encodings on `MNIST` with sensitivity probes, a simulated annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding shows that **encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success**. On the `Bot-IoT`, `CICIDS`, and `UNSW-NB15` intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations make WNN detectors label many attacks as normal traffic and raise false alarms even when aggregate accuracy stays high.

papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.
papers.summary: Imitation policies for robot manipulation trained on noisy object positions learn to discount the noisy reading, and this work quantifies by how much and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state acts as a proprioceptive anchor, and the trained policy weights the reading by alpha = V/(V + s^2), where s^2 is the reading noise and V is the learner's anchor error variance. Measured once, V predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two `robomimic` tasks with **mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression**. The discount does not carry over to closed-loop deployment, where sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded alpha in all 15 qualifying policies; all tests were pre-registered and all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

papers.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.
papers.summary: Runtime monitors for long-running autonomous agents, such as turn limits and keyword filters, can stop runs that would have succeeded or let failing runs continue. `LeBet` (Learn then Bet) learns an interpretable OR-of-AND rule monitor via stochastic local search and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening once the evidence crosses a threshold. The authors derive finite-sample guarantees on false positives and detection power while using the same trajectories for learning and calibration, without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. On `SWE-bench Lite` with `Ministral 3 8B`, the learned monitor **saves 34.46% of input-plus-output tokens** while raising output precision from 18.33% to 21.59%, at an empirical false-positive rate of 13.64%.

papers.title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.
papers.summary: Forecasting models that combine sensed time series with external text are tested here on how they behave when the text agrees or conflicts with the historical trend. `ACU-Bench` contains 1,762 real-world text-window pairs from weather, Wikipedia traffic, and finance data, each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified, and is used to evaluate ten pretrained models zero-shot. Text that directly forecasts the target helps when aligned but pushes most models' error above the no-text baseline when conflicting, and an error decomposition attributes this to oversized revisions. A training-free rule that limits revision size beats forecasts both with and without text for the four affected models, **lowering mean absolute scaled error (MASE) by 4.49%-21.98%** and raising directional accuracy by 2.99%-9.71%.

papers.title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
papers.abstract: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.
papers.summary: Evaluating complete game generation with a single aggregate score hides which capabilities an agent actually implemented. `OCTAVE` is a benchmark of 180 HTML5 game generation tasks and 1,800 evaluation requirements organized around eight capability dimensions, spanning PC and mobile web and 2D and 3D, with requirements split into Completeness (publicly specified core features) and Richness (hidden, deeper system relationships) and judged by static source-code analysis. Across 11 model-harness combinations, average scores are **33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness**, with 19.9% of generation records failing static gates or missing artifacts, and even the best combination stays below 50% on both. Systems do relatively better on core rules and numerical design, and worse on AI/NPC behavior and on feedback and game feel.

papers.title: Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved job-shop benchmark instances
papers.abstract: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.
papers.summary: The study tests whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with only open-source tools, can write scheduling heuristics that match commercial solvers in quality and speed, with every run reported and every schedule independently verified. On the 100,000-operation job shop instance `tai_100_1000_1`, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below the results of `OptalCP`, `Hexaly`, and `CP Optimizer`, and unchanged it improved all ten instances of that family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation it ended **0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for `CP Optimizer` and 2.4-4.4% for `Hexaly`**. Agent-written solvers also improved 11 of 32 open `Behnke-Geiger` flexible job shop instances and seven of ten `MKT` instances with transport robots.

papers.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, and end-to-end latency dropping from 440 to 159 minutes, with scenario-analysis recall rising from 45% to 93%. Two other domains were taken over by teams that did not write the assets, one in four days and one in seven days. A controlled ablation separates the two failure sources. The code is available at https://github.com/ZTE-AICloud/Co-Sight/tree/master/Co-Sight%20Harness.
papers.summary: Long business workflows run by language model agents fail as errors accumulate over many steps and as the knowledge a step needs is phrased differently from the user's request. `Co-Sight Harness` keeps the model fixed and moves the workflow definition, state, and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model, enforced by a state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates, with an independent auditor grading each trace and asset updates requiring a regression check and human approval. On one of three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps, a 120-case evaluation shows **unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%**, retrieval recall rising from 56% to 91.67%, and end-to-end latency falling from 440 to 159 minutes. Teams that did not write the assets took over the other two domains in four and seven days.

papers.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
papers.abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.
papers.summary: Short-term forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a, an indicator of marine phytoplankton, is computationally expensive with conventional numerical models that couple physical transport and biology. `ChlCast` is a deep learning model that produces daily forecasts over a 10-day horizon at roughly 4-km resolution between 60°S and 60°N, using factorized spatiotemporal convolutions in a multiscale architecture trained on historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatology. Against the operational 0.25° Copernicus global biogeochemical forecasting system, it **reduces mean absolute error by 70.74%** and root mean square error by 47.63% on satellite-derived fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% on independent `BGC-Argo` in situ observations. Coastal case studies show that the finer grid retains gradients and localized maxima that coarse-grid averaging weakens.

papers.title: Cross-Linguistic Acoustic Biomarkers of Cognitive Impairment Across Interactive and Single-Speaker Speech Tasks
papers.abstract: Multilingual dementia detection is essential for scalable and equitable screening. In recent years, automated speech analysis has emerged as a promising approach for supporting dementia detection by enabling non-invasive and scalable assessment of cognitive function. However, existing studies that use automated speech analysis often rely on one type of task, such as picture description, and use black-box models. These studies often neglect the role of task and language. To address these gaps, we performed a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis that integrates a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across four languages (Spanish, Mandarin, English, Japanese). We applied statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and machine learning model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets while maintaining classification performance. This enabled systematic comparison of cognitive impairment-relevant features across datasets and tasks. Our results revealed that acoustic features did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages. Temporal features remained robust across all datasets, consistently capturing timing disruption regardless of language or task. In contrast, speech rate showed strong task dependence -- emerging as informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content and pacing, but becoming less reliable when speech content was highly individualized. Pitch-related features further exhibited language-specific patterns, favoring chroma-related features in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin) and F0-related features in non-tonal languages. These findings caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and underscore the need for interpretable, context-aware approaches to multilingual dementia detection using automated speech analysis.
papers.summary: Speech-based dementia detection studies often rely on a single task type and black-box models, leaving the effect of task and language unclear. The authors run a cross-linguistic, cross-task acoustic analysis combining a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks in Spanish, Mandarin, English, and Japanese, using statistical, clinician-guided, and model-based feature selection to derive compact feature sets. They find that **acoustic features do not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages**: temporal features stay robust everywhere, speech rate is informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content, and pitch features split between chroma-related features for tonal languages and F0-related features for non-tonal ones. The results caution against pooling heterogeneous speech data indiscriminately.

papers.title: Federated Soft Poly-Level Learning Over a Distributed Network with Guaranteed Convergence
papers.abstract: Multi-level learning/optimization, e.g., bilevel optimization, has been recognized for its versatile applicability across a broad array of domains, spanning from signal processing to machine learning. However, most existing works focus on bilevel and trilevel optimization. In contrast, multi-level optimization problems involving four or more hierarchical levels, which we term poly-level learning (PLL) problems, remain largely unexplored.In addition, in practical PLL, data may be distributed across multiple nodes over a distributed network. Nevertheless, extant studies on PLL predominantly focus on the non-federated setting, necessitating the collection of data to central servers and thereby posing potential privacy risks. To this end, we propose a Federated Poly-Level Learning (FPLL) framework over a distributed network to tackle the PLL problems with soft constraints in a federated manner. FPLL hinges on a novel non-linear cut, i.e., $L$-cut, for the level-wise relaxation to the PLL problems. Additionally, the proposed federated algorithm is designed with adjustable parameters that allow for a flexible trade-off between its computational complexity and performance efficiency, enabling users to tune it according to specific application requirements. We also carry out non-asymptotic analysis to derive the iteration complexity for the proposed FPLL to achieve the $\epsilon$-Pareto stationary point. Extensive experiments have been undertaken to elucidate the superior efficacy of the proposed method.
papers.summary: Multi-level optimization research has concentrated on bilevel and trilevel problems, leaving problems with four or more hierarchical levels, termed poly-level learning (PLL), largely unexplored, especially when data is spread across nodes. The proposed Federated Poly-Level Learning framework (`FPLL`) handles PLL problems with soft constraints over a distributed network, using a new non-linear cut called the `L-cut` to relax the problem level by level, with adjustable parameters that trade computational cost against performance. A non-asymptotic analysis gives **the iteration complexity needed to reach an epsilon-Pareto stationary point**, and experiments are reported to support the method's effectiveness.

papers.title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
papers.abstract: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter interference bound: smaller $(\alpha, \beta)$ provably yields lower parameter interference through better spectral alignment. To exploit such a proxy, we augment the training objective with a proxy regularizer. Evaluating this regularizer during fine-tuning requires a concrete mechanism. We study three instantiations, including (J) an exact evaluation via Jacobian-vector products, (F) a frozen curvature approximation using the Fisher information matrix, and (O) an output-drift formulation that constrains the model's functional deviation on the proxy directly. We prove that all three coincide under the NTK linearization, where existing analyses of such regularizers stop, and go further to characterize standard non-linear fine-tuning, bounding how far each instantiation departs from its linearized reference and obtain a three-way hierarchy, zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O). Empirical validation on the commonly used vision-language model CLIP confirms these theoretical predictions.
papers.summary: Model merging builds multi-task models without joint training but suffers from parameter interference, and fixes that regularize fine-tuning with other tasks' data break the independence and privacy assumptions of merging. This framework characterizes when a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can stand in for that data, using spectral coverage (alpha) and leakage (beta) to derive an interference bound in which smaller values provably give lower interference. Three ways of computing the proxy regularizer are analyzed: exact Jacobian-vector products, a frozen Fisher information approximation, and an output-drift constraint. All three coincide under neural tangent kernel (NTK) linearization, while under standard non-linear fine-tuning **their departure from the linearized reference follows a three-way hierarchy: zero for the Jacobian form, proxy-independent for Fisher, and scaling with proxy quality for output drift**, which experiments on `CLIP` confirm.

papers.title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
papers.abstract: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.
papers.summary: Forecasting systems built on large language models (LLMs) often produce probabilities for related events that violate the axioms of probability, and naive fixes such as projecting onto the set of consistent forecasts can hurt accuracy. The authors fine-tune a supervisory language model that reads the reasoning behind each forecast and uses it to reconcile inconsistencies while also improving accuracy. On `ForecastBench`, the method **improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented `GPT-5.1` forecaster by 9.3% while reducing structural inconsistency measures by 82-90%**. Across the baselines and ablations tested, no alternative matched both gains at once.

papers.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.
papers.summary: Local large language model (LLM) servers typically serve one runtime on one machine, which fits poorly when several agents share a model with an interactive user or when a team owns several machines from different vendors. `Superfluid` is an open-source server that drives `llama.cpp`, `MLX`, or `BaseRT` in isolated worker processes behind one scheduler that prioritizes interactive requests over agent work, computes shared prompts once, and writes every token to a durable log; across devices it exposes a fleet as a single API endpoint, routing work by measured speed and tolerating machines joining or failing. For `Qwen3.8-27B` on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working gets its **first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on `llama-server`, `Ollama`, and `mlx_lm.server`**. On six machines from three chip vendors it answered all 5,041 requests while machines joined and one was killed, and on twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustained 10,656 tokens per second across 38,563 requests without a failure.

papers.title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
papers.abstract: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.
papers.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) approaches to creative product design offer little control over implicit, product-specific constraints such as brand image. Given a product name, the proposed framework builds a brand image survey report from product and market information, derives a creative direction from it, and feeds that direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts revised. On 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, judged by a vision-language model for creativity and brand identifiability, it achieves **a more favorable trade-off between creativity and brand identifiability** than naive T2I, `IP-Adapter`/`IT-Blender`, and unconstrained self-enhancement on the same backbone. Gains are clearest in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle.

papers.title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models
papers.abstract: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history branch yields 42/46 correct responses, compared with 16/46 under full history. A matched cue-placement control changes false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in Qwen 3.5 4B. Twelve independently authored pressure templates demonstrate substantial sensitivity to wording. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of KAD for evaluating factual reliability beyond initial susceptibility, enabling systematic comparisons of false-answer persistence, recovery conditions and conversational interventions.
papers.summary: When a language model accepts a false correction during a factual discussion, what it says next depends on how the conversation continues, which a single susceptibility score does not capture. Knowledge Answer Divergence (`KAD`) is an evaluation protocol that freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false answer and branches independent probes from that exact history, separating initial adoption from later persistence, recovery, and abstention. Across eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, a neutral-history branch for `Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B` yields **42/46 correct responses, compared with 16/46 under full history**. A matched cue-placement control shifts false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in `Qwen 3.5 4B`, and twelve independently authored pressure templates show substantial sensitivity to wording.

papers.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
papers.abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.
papers.summary: `GDP_xlsx` is a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace spreadsheet requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with the full workbook or CSV file and an expert rubric of binary criteria, totaling 2.18 million populated cells and 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric, including completeness and exclusivity criteria that require set-valued answers to be found in full with nothing extra. Models are ranked by strict pass@1, the share of attempts meeting every criterion. Across 20 model configurations from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top scorer, `Gemini 4 Argon`, **passes only 38.3% of attempts**, with a median of 19.3%; the harness and three tasks are public while the other 67 are held out.

papers.title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
papers.abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.
papers.summary: An audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella has a large language model, seeded with the original text, feed endlessly on its own output, and the authors examine how the text drifts into narrative deviations, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long incoherent stretches. Activation steering, including a new adaptive steering method, is used to control the rhythm of the narrative and of the model's digressions over long generations. The authors report that **the steering is simultaneously effective and unpredictable**, which they present as reflecting a gap between the perceived interpretability of AI systems and actual control over them.

papers.title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
papers.abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.
papers.summary: The Thomson problem asks for the minimum Coulomb energy arrangement of N unit charges on a sphere, with the best-known large-N configurations curated in the `Cambridge Cluster Database`. Using a search pipeline built and run with large language model agents (`Claude` via chat and `Claude Code`), combining replica-exchange basin hopping, a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions, and gradient-only polishing, the authors report **lower-energy configurations for N = 912, 1382, and 2502, certified by exact integer arithmetic**. They report every search including failures, such as two spurious records caused by not comparing candidates against polished database energies, and a speed-up that passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison. Three practices are distilled for agent-driven computational discovery: verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare against a polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.
papers.highlight_summary:
Three large-N entries in the `Cambridge Cluster Database` of best-known Thomson-problem configurations (minimum Coulomb energy for N unit charges on a sphere) are improved by a search pipeline that the authors built and ran with `Claude` and `Claude Code`, while the humans chose the problem, sizes and stop rules. Every search is reported, including the failed ones, and the failures are turned into practices for trusting agent-assisted computational discovery.

- The search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations with full `L-BFGS` relaxation, a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling points by geometry, and gradient-only Barzilai–Borwein polishing.
- New configurations for N=912, 1382 and 2502 sit **0.0036186**, **0.0109730** and **0.0614033** below the database energies (relative decreases of about **1e-8**), certified by exact integer arithmetic on rationalised coordinates with enclosures narrower than 3e-18, and all three are numerically strict local minima with the same defect inventory and scar compositions as the database entries.
- A local-relaxation speed-up designed by the chat assistant passed its 1e-9 exactness test yet found nothing in **4 core-hours** of a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within **15 minutes**, after about 72 core-hours had already been spent on it across 11 sizes.
- Polishing alone lowered the unconverged database entries for N=3552 and N=5872 by 1.50e-5 and 1.23e-5, more than the pipeline's 1e-5 candidate threshold, which produced **two spurious records** until candidates were compared with the polished baseline.
- The authors claim neither global optimality nor superiority over the October 2026 method that set the largest entries, since they ran no equal-budget comparison, only **3 of 11** sizes searched with full relaxation improved, the final N=2502 configuration depended on a single run, and recombination supplied only the last 7% of that decrease.

papers.title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql
papers.summary: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are accurate at text-to-SQL but slow and costly, and they send sensitive queries to external APIs. `LuthorSQL` is a non-autoregressive 7B model that acts as a fast first-pass gate, escalating to a slower agent only when uncertain: a single forward pass predicts slot scores over a bounded query-plan grammar, up to 32 candidate plans are compiled and run, and a trained validator picks the answer. Alone it reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on the `BIRD` hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on one GPU, keeps that accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit weights, and transfers zero-shot to five other SQL dialects within 3.1 points. In a pre-registered confidence cascade with `Claude Opus 5.5` over 227 questions on post-cutoff databases, it answers nearly half of the questions locally and **cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy**; contamination probing also finds that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema.

papers.title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
papers.abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes.
