In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.
papers.summary: When a Go model picks a different move from the expert, the usual measure is how far apart the two moves are on the board, which says little about whether they have similar effects. Transition Representation Consistency (`TReC`) plays both moves from the same position and takes the cosine similarity between the two resulting changes in a board-state embedding. With a frozen `KataGo` network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the per-position gap between the best and worst candidate had a median of **0.88 to 1.33 for `TReC` versus 0.01 to 0.08 for a direct successor-state cosine**, depending on the layer. `TReC` tracked coordinate distance only weakly, with a median within-position rank correlation of -0.19.

papers.title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
papers.abstract: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.
papers.summary: Implicit neural video representations are slow to fit, which limits their practical use. `Q-GAS` combines multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids, a compact quadratic-gating decoder in the style of SwiGLU, and a sampler that mixes uniform samples with samples from a periodically refreshed high-error pool, so no auxiliary model is needed to predict hard samples. On the `UVG` Beauty, Bosphorus and Jockey sequences it **fits and quantizes in under 50 seconds on one RTX PRO 6000** and decodes at over 370 frames per second with mixed precision. The authors report training 5.5 to 7.2 times faster than their `Instant-NGP` baseline and 19 to 28 times faster than `RNeRV`, with better quality than `NeRV`-family pipelines at comparable bitrate under a 90-second budget.

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
papers.abstract: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.
papers.summary: Directly editing the weights of a pretrained detector without gradients is an alternative to fine-tuning, and it is unclear whether guidance from a large language model (LLM) helps. Across five experimental phases on `YOLO26` models and `MS COCO`, the study compares deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, `CMA-ES`, proposals from a local LLM, and a hybrid LLM-`CMA-ES` method against a matched random-policy control. Gains on the 1,000-image development subset did not carry over to a disjoint 1,500-image subset, and **the hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance** (p = 0.612, 0.369 and 0.694 at budgets of 8, 25 and 50 evaluations). A five-seed `YOLO26m` replication gave an average-precision difference of +0.004 points, with a 95% confidence interval spanning zero.

papers.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) training of language models is unstable and usually needs a researcher watching the run, which makes it hard to automate. `AutoRL` is a multi-agent system that supervises a run in progress: Perceptor agents monitor training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation and efficiency, three Proposer agents diagnose problems and refine interventions, and an Orchestrator applies approved changes through hot updates or by resuming from a checkpoint. In experiments on `Qwen3` and `LongCat-Flash-Lite`, the authors report that **`AutoRL` outperforms static RL recipes and a general-purpose agent**. They conclude that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment.

papers.title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
papers.abstract: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.
papers.summary: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of its fixed dataset, and augmenting that data faces a trade-off: generating each agent's trajectory independently gives diversity without coordination, while joint generation gives coordination but reproduces the training distribution. `MASTARS` is a diffusion-based framework that generates trajectories one agent at a time and uses inpainting to keep them consistent across agents. The authors report that **the augmented data improves several offline MARL methods** on the `MPE`, `SMAC` and `SMAC-v2` benchmarks.

papers.title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
papers.abstract: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.
papers.summary: Daily benchmarks of GPU rental prices can break down when marketplace quotes are missing. This study stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four recovery methods, using 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations across 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days. Whole-source outages cut publication coverage to 0.77 with zero error on the dates that were published, whereas **missing quotes that change the benchmark's composition kept 0.86 coverage but introduced 7.74 log points of error**. A rule that withholds publication based on observable signals improved the main error-coverage criterion in none of 10 cases, and the results concern asking prices, not transaction prices.

papers.title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.
papers.summary: Coding agents that work from images or must check visual output are limited by their own built-in vision, and text-only agents have none. Vision-as-a-Tool (`VaaT`) treats general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as external utilities the agent can call, so a text-only agent can offload visual reasoning and a vision-capable agent can supplement its own perception. The paradigm is implemented in `VHarness`, a framework built on five atomic actions, and evaluated on Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG and Image-to-3D generation. The authors report that **`VHarness` improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for both text-only and multimodal coding agents**.

papers.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
papers.abstract: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.
papers.summary: Service robots need to recognise individual users from only a few observations, even as appearance, background noise and speech content change. The proposed model learns person concepts without identity labels using a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process, combining visual, acoustic and linguistic features from Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (`CLIP`) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (`CLAP`) reduced by principal component analysis (PCA). In tests with six participants under eight conditions, it reached **0.89 average identification accuracy while inferring the number of people itself**, comparable to the 0.88 of k-means clustering given the true number. The model was also demonstrated on a `Toyota Human Support Robot`.

papers.title: Can Agents Keep Up with Time? An Empirical Analysis of Temporal Adaptation After a Conversational Hiatus
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.
papers.summary: Users of persistent assistant agents often return to a conversation after a long gap, during which scheduled dates may have passed while the stored records stay unchanged. This study builds session-rekindling tasks that hold the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and how temporal information reaches the agent, tested across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions. **Agents reliably query the clock and even note that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event.** Supplying explicit temporal context reduces the error, and providing the computed relation between the dates removes it entirely.

papers.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.
papers.summary: As a long-running LLM agent's interaction history grows, summarizing can drop exact details needed later, while keeping whole interactions carries a lot of irrelevant material. `CarryOn` is a lightweight context manager that pairs a compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence, using a learned selector and an adaptive retention policy that need no extra LLM calls. Across `AppWorld`, `OfficeBench` and `Tau2 Telecom` with three actor models, it reaches **75.7% macro-averaged task success, 6.7 percentage points above the strongest baseline**. It also scores best on average on two metrics the authors introduce, one weighting success against resource use and one measuring normalized cost per success (NCS).

papers.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.
papers.summary: Conversational shopping agents face user demand that shifts over time and a tool and skill harness that keeps changing, so a model trained once falls behind and manual retraining is slow. `G-CAST` is a continual self-training system that turns daily production evidence into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data, evolves its reward under governance, and gates each checkpoint update on cumulative evaluation. On a production e-commerce agent, the authors report that **it adapts better to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior** than an autonomous post-training baseline. The system is deployed in `Yuancai`, a business-to-business procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

papers.title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
papers.abstract: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.
papers.summary: Chest computed tomography (CT) scans from lung screening carry information about both lung cancer and cardiovascular risk, but clinical calculators treat each disease separately and ignore CT findings, while unconstrained machine learning overfits small cohorts. `CE-Agent` (Causal Envelope Agent) is a two-stage framework that first turns published epidemiological evidence into constraints on risk-factor weights, then estimates baseline risk and CT phenotypes from cohort data, with closed-form uncertainty propagation for missing inputs. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, it outperforms cardiovascular calculators and **corrects a 1.7-fold risk overestimation by the `Pooled Cohort Equations`**. The authors also report that it lowers required sample sizes up to fivefold and matches established lung cancer screening models.

papers.title: Aligning AI Teams
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.
papers.summary: Alignment training on a single LLM agent can fail to carry over when agents work in teams, and this study looks at why and what restores it, using two software-engineering tasks and ten consulting-proposal tasks. The gap between single-agent and team safety shows no clear trend with model capability, and interventions such as peer critique or group chat coordination do not reliably close it. **Diffusion of responsibility accounts for much of the gap**: agents in teams are less likely to check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize or deflect issues. Appointing a safety lead agent and having a coordinator publish a safety specification restored single-agent behavior, and the authors release `magelab`, a multi-agent orchestration and experimentation framework.

papers.title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
papers.abstract: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.
papers.summary: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine is difficult because its planning, construction tools and stored experience often depend on the original backend. `SceneAgent` is a multi-agent framework that keeps the evolving world in a canonical `SceneContext`, isolates engine specifics in backend adapters, and distills human-approved construction traces into reusable layout and content skills. On `GameSceneBench`, a new set of 69 indoor and outdoor prompts, it obtains **human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2 to 89.4% against five baselines**. Deployment in a second engine kept the construction protocol and skill library and replaced only the backend integration components.

papers.title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
papers.summary: Video encoders such as `V-JEPA` capture how scenes change, but once connected to a language model trained on captions, that information goes unused: a linear probe reads speed from frozen `V-JEPA` features at 87% while the combined model answers at chance. The authors show that dynamics sit in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders but not for text-aligned encoders such as `SigLIP`, and they build counterfactual supervision by applying pixel transformations that create answer-balanced video variants. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples, the resulting `V-JEPA-LM` models lead every size class across eleven video benchmarks, with **the 4B model scoring 72.1 against 61.1 for the best open 4B model**. At a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on speed questions.

papers.title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
papers.abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.
papers.summary: Abliteration removes refusal behavior from open-weight language models by editing weights without fine-tuning, and the developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (`ARA`) has reported that the simpler direction-based form increasingly fails on newer models. This study edits five pairs of older and newer releases from the `Qwen`, `Gemma`, `OLMo` and `Mistral Small` families in `Heretic` 2.0 under matched prompts and budgets, with the `WildGuard` judge scoring refusals on 972 held-out harmful prompts. **Refusal removal did not become uniformly harder**: newer releases kept between -1 and +37 percentage points more refusal after direction-based removal and between -26 and +34 after `ARA`. The outcome depended on the release pair, method and budget, and each `ARA` verdict rests on a single run.

papers.title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Ni\~{n}o Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
papers.abstract: The predictability of the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Ni\~{n}o, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Ni\~{n}o development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.
papers.summary: Forecast errors for the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) are usually attributed to large-scale errors in initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Applying the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method to a differentiable ocean AI model, the authors find that **these errors can originate from mesoscale errors in initial ocean currents**. The most influential current errors differ by event, lying in the eastern Pacific for the 1997/98 El Niño and the western Pacific for 2015/16. The fastest error growth coincides with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO.

papers.title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
papers.abstract: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.
papers.summary: Automated interpretability pipelines use LLMs both to generate and to evaluate explanations of a model's internal features, which makes it hard to validate the explanations or tell whether a failure comes from the extracted representations or from the explaining model. `DECODE` is a visual analytics system that brings human review back into this process through three diagnostic stages, separating structural defects from explanation-level misalignments. It uses agreement among independently generated explanations as a proxy for reliability, and an active seeding protocol to recommend which instances to review by hand. In a case study on **16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features**, the authors report that it identifies and attributes interpretability failures at scale.
papers.highlight_summary:
Automated interpretability pipelines let LLMs both write and grade explanations of sparse autoencoder features with no ground truth, so failures are hard to detect or trace to the SAE versus the explainer. `DECODE` is a visual analytics system that puts a human back in the loop, using agreement among independent explainers and metrics as a proxy for reliability.

- The diagnosis runs in three stages (structural soundness, explanation adequacy, failure attribution) that sort each feature into one of five categories: `Incoherent Splitting`, `Well-Explained`, `Missed Syntax`, `Missed Context`, or `Noisy Activation`.
- Evidence per feature comes from three explainers (`Llama 3.1 70B`, `GPT-4o mini`, `Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite`) and three metrics (fuzz, detection, embedding), while a three-phase active seeding protocol picks features for manual review and an SVM propagates those labels to the rest.
- In a case study on **16,384** features from the `Gemma-2-9b` layer-31 SAE, three experts each finished the pipeline in about two hours with 138–168 manual labels, finding **45–51%** of features `Well-Explained` and `Noisy Activation` the dominant failure.
- Individual experts barely beat a score-only baseline on macro-F1 (**0.40, 0.37, 0.41** versus **0.36**), but pooling all three reached **0.62**, and experts recovered `Noisy Activation` at 67–87% recall against the baseline's 10%.
- Label propagation is the weak link, scoring only **0.23–0.29** macro-F1 against 0.60–0.65 for manual labels, and the 233-feature reference set was adjudicated by a single author with LLM assistance rather than being independent ground truth.

papers.title: AI-aided Decision-Making in Education - Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility
papers.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based systems have become increasingly integrated into various aspects of everyday life, including education, understanding how these systems make decisions is of paramount importance. AI holds significant potential to enhance educational practices through the facilitation of personalized and adaptive learning, automation of assessment procedures, and assistance with administrative tasks. However, the opacity of AI-based decision-making in education (especially with deep learning and generative AI models) can hamper decision-making, especially when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. In this chapter, we argue that three key principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings. Acknowledging the inherent uncertainties in AI-based decisions, analogous to those in human decision-making, is fundamental. Explainability is critical for ensuring that the functioning and outcomes of AI applications are transparent and comprehensible to both educators and learners. Furthermore, human responsibility is crucial, particularly in human decision-making, which remains indispensable across all stages of AI development and deployment. By examining these three principles, this chapter provides a comprehensive guide for stakeholders seeking to integrate AI thoughtfully and effectively into the educational system.
papers.summary: AI systems used in education for personalized learning, automated assessment and administrative tasks often make decisions that are opaque, which is a problem when outcomes look unjustified or wrong. This book chapter argues that **three principles are essential for legitimate use of AI in education: uncertainty, explainability and human responsibility**. It discusses acknowledging the uncertainty in AI decisions, making their functioning comprehensible to educators and learners, and keeping humans responsible at every stage of development and deployment.

papers.title: FlexCast: Flexible Context Learning for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) based on autoregressive (AR) next-token prediction entangle two factors: variable-context conditioning and prediction-unit factorization with autoregressive rollout. Strong AR performance therefore does not reveal whether generalization stems from the flexible training distribution, the local prediction target, the left-to-right inference process, or their combination. We propose FlexCast, a flexible context-target learning framework that disentangles these factors. FlexCast reformulates forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches: during pretraining, it dynamically samples visible context and masked target patches, exposing the model to diverse context-target configurations without sequential decoding. At inference time, the same pretrained model supports one-step forecasting, confidence-based iterative refinement, and next-token-style generation through a unified mask-and-predict interface, enabling controlled comparison of inference schedules under identical architecture, data, and objective. Evaluated on BLAST and multiple zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast achieves accuracy competitive with or better than strong TSFM baselines while substantially reducing inference latency. Ablations confirm that context diversity and contiguous target masking drive performance, while left-to-right decoding does not yield consistent gains once flexible context-target relationships have been learned, suggesting that the key benefit of AR-style TSFMs lies in flexible training rather than sequential inference. The code is available at https://github.com/BenchCouncil/FlexCast.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) built on autoregressive next-token prediction mix together several factors, so it is unclear whether their generalization comes from flexible training contexts, the local prediction target, or left-to-right decoding. `FlexCast` recasts forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches, sampling visible context and masked targets during pretraining, so one model supports one-step forecasting, iterative refinement and next-token-style generation. On `BLAST` and several zero-shot benchmarks it is competitive with or better than strong baselines while substantially reducing inference latency. Ablations indicate that **left-to-right decoding yields no consistent gains once flexible context-target relationships are learned**.

papers.title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries
papers.abstract: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.
papers.summary: Writing temporal-logic formulas that capture intended behaviour is hard, and existing active-learning methods require a teacher to answer equivalence queries and construct counterexamples. The proposed framework for `LTLf` asks the teacher only to label traces and answer natural-language questions, while the learner keeps an enumerated version space of candidate formulas and generates traces that distinguish them. The authors prove consistency, bounded-query identification, and a PAC guarantee. With a simulated teacher on 36 targets, the learner **identifies every target with fewer than seven queries on average beyond an initial sample of ten traces**, and runs faster than the SAT-based approach at every target size.

papers.title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
papers.abstract: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.
papers.summary: Encoder models can pick one of several options in a single forward pass without generating text, and this technical report compares four recipes for fine-tuning `UltraBERT-380M` with one mask per option. Trained on the same data as a `Qwen3-0.6B` decoder using the `LLM-as-Jev` recipe (67.6% test accuracy), **the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%**, with the largest gain coming from scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" rather than "yes" alone. On an NVIDIA A100 with one request at a time, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, though it uses more peak memory (2.8 versus 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head also predicts, in the same pass, which sentences support the answer.

papers.title: OmniScore-Bench: Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Musical Score Reading
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but their ability to recognise notation, recover its structure and interpret its musical meaning requires separate evaluation. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) resources establish detection and transcription measurements; a transcription score alone leaves the strengths and bottlenecks of a VLM score reader unresolved. We introduce OmniScore-Bench, an evaluation of OMR capabilities in VLMs through 3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Each question specifies a visible scope, reference annotations and an answer schema, enabling automatic evaluation from symbol localisation to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering. Our assessment of twelve VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses examine the roles of score images, auxiliary givens and additional page context. On the tested subset, image removal exposes visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation while measuring how much performance remains with public context alone. Separate format and content analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors. OmniScore-Bench supports diagnosing which score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably and which require improvement.
papers.summary: Transcription scores alone do not reveal where vision-language models (VLMs) succeed or fail at reading musical scores. `OmniScore-Bench` evaluates optical music recognition (OMR) abilities through **3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes**, each with a defined visible scope, reference annotations, and an answer schema for automatic scoring. An assessment of twelve VLMs finds operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page, and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses with the image removed expose visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation, and separate answer-format violations from musical errors.

papers.title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
papers.abstract: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. Although existing studies have made progress, they are limited by data and methodological gaps. Existing studies are largely predictive for existing cities rather than generative for future cities; fine-grained, aligned monthly dynamic energy data are scarce; and existing GenAI models struggle to generate dynamic urban functional monthly energy. We present DySENSE, a joint multimodal GenAI framework that synthesizes static urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned, dynamic monthly building energy consumption maps. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. By conditioning on dynamic monthly and climate prompts, DySENSE can jointly generate dynamic, monthly energy consumption maps while keeping the urban morphology static. Experiments across four cities (New York, Washington, Norfolk, Busan) demonstrated that DySENSE can generate annotated high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data, boosting downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU, and achieving strong energy dynamic consistency. Compared to existing methods, DySENSE significantly improved prediction performance (8.7% accuracy) and reduced prediction error (9%-18% CVRMSE, ASHRAE). DySENSE offers an effective foundation for energy-efficient cities, peak-load analysis, building performance simulation and dynamic demand response for city, energy, and building science. The data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skl24/MUSE2 and https://github.com/kailaisun/DySENSE
papers.summary: Fine-grained, aligned monthly building-energy data for cities is scarce, and existing generative models struggle to produce dynamic energy maps. `DySENSE` is a joint multimodal generative framework that synthesizes urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned monthly energy-consumption maps, decoupling static urban morphology (conditioned on land use) from dynamic energy use (conditioned on month and climate prompts). Across New York, Washington, Norfolk, and Busan, it generates annotated synthetic data using less than 25% labelled data, **boosting downstream prediction by 8% mIoU**, and reduces prediction error by 9% to 18% CVRMSE compared with existing methods.

papers.title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or steps to reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are judged by their final outputs. In linear regression models the authors derive exact criteria for when sharing helps by balancing variance savings against bias, characterize final-output risk under a fixed linear propagation map, and give conditional end-to-end error bounds for general routed computations. They **construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error**, and confirm such a reversal in controlled experiments. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers show statistically supported one-step gains under teacher forcing without statistically resolved gains in free-running final outputs.

papers.title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.
papers.summary: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must both complete the task and obey domain policies, and blocking an unsafe action can leave the agent stranded with no way to recover. `Soteria` has the agent generate a structured hierarchical plan that is formally verified against the specifications before any tool is invoked, then uses that plan at runtime both to keep trajectories conformant and to guide recovery when an action is blocked. Across multiple tool-use benchmarks, it achieves **1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines with no policy violations**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Runtime guardrails for LLM agents can block a policy-violating tool call but leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover, so safety comes at the cost of task completion. `Soteria` has the agent write a plan that is formally verified against domain policies before any tool runs, then uses that plan as both the execution roadmap and the recovery guide when a runtime monitor blocks a call.

- The planner writes each plan in a DSL as a guarded transition system composed from reusable, pre-verified sub-plans, and `Dafny` checks tool-contract preconditions, progress (no dead ends) and policy compliance, with up to 8 repair retries and a fallback to the strongest partially verified plan.
- At runtime a `SpecMonitor` checks every proposed tool call against the trace so far and blocks any that would violate a specification, while the plan is shown to the executor as a progressively simplified worklist that points to the next valid step.
- Across 207 tasks from `τ²-Airline`, `τ²-Retail` and a `Toolathlon` subset with four backbone models, it reaches **100% conformance with zero violations** (baselines peak at 93%) and averages **1.7×** the best baseline's conformance-gated success rate, with `Claude Opus 4.6` at **88.0%** and **90.4%** on Airline and Retail versus 56.0% and 46.5%.
- Ablations on `τ²-Airline` show that verification and sub-plans alone still leave 10–24 violations and only the monitor removes them, while sub-plans raise the share of plans that verify from 38 of 60 planning turns to **65 of 68**.
- The guarantee is only as good as the specifications, which are LLM-drafted and then hand-validated over a few hours per benchmark (24–41 formulas), and replanning every dialogue turn makes it roughly 2–4× costlier per task on the conversational benchmarks, while `Toolathlon` success stays low at 9.3–18.6%.

papers.title: Photogrammetric 3D Model-Based Animal Behavior Classification
papers.abstract: Video-based behavior estimation is often implemented end-to-end from image sequences. We advocate a two-stage alternative: reconstruct 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior. This makes ambiguities of the ill-posed 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. We demonstrate the strategy with simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.
papers.summary: Video-based behavior estimation is usually done end-to-end from image sequences. The authors argue for a two-stage alternative that **reconstructs 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior**, which makes the ambiguities of the 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. They demonstrate the strategy on simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.

papers.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems delegate subtasks to agents and combine their responses with an aggregation rule, which lets a malicious agent steer the final answer. The authors introduce response manipulation attacks (`ReMA`), which iteratively refine malicious responses using feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system, and a defense called `SecMAS` that selects the response most semantically consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the others. They prove security guarantees for `SecMAS` against untargeted and targeted attacks. In evaluations, existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to `ReMA`, whereas **`SecMAS` defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants, at comparable utility**.

papers.title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow
papers.summary: Predicting spatial transcriptomics (ST), meaning spatially resolved gene expression, from histology images is typically done with complicated architectures and limited to small fixed gene panels. `GeneFlow` combines flow-matching generative modeling with multimodal fusion of histology and gene tokens, predicting gene expression directly rather than an intermediate velocity field while still training with a velocity-based objective. It reports state-of-the-art results across multiple ST benchmarks, with **up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction**, while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Adversarially Attacking Symbolic Vocabulary Vulnerabilities In LLM Planners
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, their abilities in navigating automated planning tasks have become essential. However, despite their strengths, LLMs' planning ability is not robust, particularly when they are not allowed to exploit commonsense cues in the symbolic vocabulary (e.g., names of actions, predicates, and objects) used to define planning tasks. This makes LLMs unreliable compared to symbolic planners. With recent reasoning models showing improved planning performance on tasks with obfuscated symbolic vocabularies, we utilize an adversarial attack framework to reveal to what extent the crucial weaknesses of LLM agents at joint symbolic interpretation and planning remain and whether they can reason properly when presented with severe cases. As such, our main contribution is devising an LLM-based attack model, which we call Symbolic Swapper, to automatically generate obfuscated planning domains with non-standard symbolic vocabularies that systematically break strong reasoning models' ability to plan. In doing so, we reveal how much LLMs' planning abilities can be further degraded under more advanced obfuscation schemes, allowing us to ascertain their success when having to rely on their pure planning ability. We find that attacks can decrease the planning performance of base models and even robust planning frameworks by over 70%. We further analyze the factors behind how LLM planning abilities break down and find that successful obfuscation causes models to appear to significantly degrade in reasoning quality despite them showing some inherent ability to understand the domain, revealing a gap in the perception of a task domain and being able to plan under it.
papers.summary: LLM planners lean on commonsense cues in the names of actions, predicates, and objects, and their performance drops when that symbolic vocabulary is obfuscated. The authors build an LLM-based attack model, `Symbolic Swapper`, that automatically generates planning domains with non-standard vocabularies designed to break strong reasoning models. The attacks **decrease the planning performance of base models and even robust planning frameworks by over 70%**. Analysis indicates that models retain some ability to understand the obfuscated domain while their reasoning quality degrades, pointing to a gap between perceiving a domain and planning within it.

papers.title: SWIFT: Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Forecasting
papers.abstract: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.
papers.summary: Few-shot adaptation of time-series foundation models normally needs an extra fine-tuning dataset, which is a barrier to adoption. Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (`SWIFT`) instead specializes the model for a single prediction window using only that sample's own observed history, combining self-retrieval over the history, a frequency-aware loss, and a deviation-aware fusion step that balances adaptation against the model's general knowledge. Across 24 combinations of four backbones and six `Chronos Benchmark II` datasets, it yields **average reductions of 6.41% in MASE and 4.83% in WQL**.

papers.title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.
papers.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) teams learn coordination conventions that can become obsolete or unsafe when deployment requirements change, and the same convention can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. `CARVE` removes a specified convention by attributing it to influential interactions, applying subspace updates that limit interference with retained behaviors, training agents on counterfactual alternatives, and adversarially auditing whether the convention can still be elicited. Across five cooperative MARL benchmarks, it **reduces the mean convention-completion rate by 91.4%** and the worst-case elicitation rate by 83.3%, with a median utility loss of 5.9% and unchanged inference latency.

papers.title: Condensing Law of Security Information
papers.abstract: Scaling laws indicate that the generalization error of a large language model (LLM) decreases monotonically with model size once data is sufficient, and the corollary that larger models outperform smaller ones is now widely accepted. We argue that this corollary fails in security: decisions there hinge on anomalous inputs, which are long-tailed (e.g., zero-day attacks) and therefore poorly served by likelihood fitting. Worse still, the capability brought about by scale (e.g., inferring the intended whole from a corrupted part) leads a LLM silently \emph{repair} the anomaly before any downstream security head ever sees it. We formalize this as a tradeoff between two quantities: the cognitive capability $K(W)=I(W;P)$ that a model holds about the world distribution, and the security-information retention $R(W)=\frac{I(Z;S)}{I(A;S)}$ that survives in its intermediate representation. We derive three information-theoretic bounds to connect them: an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of $K(W)$, an upper bound on $R(W)$ in terms of the restoration error, and a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of $R(W)$. These theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted, indicating that optimal usable security information can be achieved at a certain model size. We state this as the \emph{condensing law of security information}: usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite $N^{\star}$ rather than decreasing without bound. The experiments on various real-world LLMs validate the condensing law, indicating that there is an optimal model size to solve security issues.
papers.summary: Scaling laws suggest larger language models generalize better, but the authors argue this fails for security tasks, where decisions hinge on rare anomalous inputs and a more capable model tends to silently repair the anomaly in its internal representation before a downstream security head can see it. They formalize a tradeoff between a model's knowledge of the world distribution and how much security-relevant information survives in its intermediate representation, and derive three information-theoretic bounds linking the two. The resulting condensing law states that **usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and minimized at a finite model size**. Experiments on several real-world LLMs are reported as consistent with this.

papers.title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates.
