We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.
papers.summary: An evolutionary model is used to study how selection shapes an AI agent's choices when task completion conflicts with rules of conduct: copies of an agent face an uncertain reward state and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. Long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it; a task-only policy fails once conduct matters, and a fixed linear policy drifts toward task completion as stakes rise. By contrast, **a learned policy converges to the tradeoffs its environment rewards, and accumulated experience makes this harder to reverse under later task-only training**, though finite memory weakens the protection. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate the effects of training targets and memory.

papers.title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.
papers.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) usually trains a model under a fixed, hand-written harness, the scaffold that decides what the model sees of its own interaction and what guidance it gets, even though the best harness depends on the domain, the data, and the model's changing behavior. `ModHarness-RL` instead records the interaction as typed State blocks and treats two harness components as programs over them: a Compression program that assembles history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories so the harness evolves with the model. Across `CodeSearch`, `ALFWorld`, and `BIRD SQL` with models from 1.5B to 8B parameters, the learned mechanisms **improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings**.

papers.title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
papers.abstract: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $\kappa$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $\kappa \rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\Theta(\log\kappa\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(\kappa, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.
papers.summary: Generative models built on stochastic interpolants need both a schedule bridging the initial and target distributions and a discretization of the resulting probability-flow ordinary differential equation. The authors design the two jointly using analyticity of the complexified trajectories, solving the problem exactly by conformal mapping to obtain variance-preserving elliptic schedules based on Jacobi elliptic functions, and a paired sampler, `Zoloflow`, that accounts for the target's condition number κ. For Gaussian targets, `Zoloflow` is minimax optimal among oblivious score-span algorithms, reaching total-variation error ε with **Θ(log κ · log(√d/ε)) score queries**, and for log-concave targets the elliptic schedule reaches 2-Wasserstein error ε with roughly √d · polylog(κ, 1/ε) score evaluations. Experiments on non-log-concave targets compare the elliptic schedule with alternative schedules on synthetic benchmarks and image generation datasets.

papers.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
papers.summary: Demonstrations speed up single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) one person usually cannot teleoperate several agents at once, and policies imitated from Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (`R2BC`), where the demonstrator controls one agent at a time, are capped by demonstration quality. `IBMARL` extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (`IBRL`) to cooperative teams: each agent gets one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, an ensemble of centralized critics picks among the per-agent combinations, and a gated imitation penalty pulls each RL policy toward imitation only where the critics value the imitation action more. After training, each agent runs its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative benchmarks, `IBMARL` **surpasses its imitation policies 2.6-4.2× faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks** and is the only method to surpass them on the other two, exceeds the demonstrator on two of the four, and with real human demonstrations still surpasses imitation learning alone more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

papers.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks, reading what a network does, repairing it, or writing one from scratch without gradient descent, a capability termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). `WeightBench` evaluates this with 42 tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing, and writing weights, recognizing impossible edits, and data-free compression, on networks ranging from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. `Claude Opus 5.5` reaches **a macro score of 0.535 on all 42 tasks** (`Sonnet 5.5` 0.466, `Haiku 5.5` 0.402, `DeepSeek v4-flash` 0.215), while `GPT-6.1-sol` scores 0.568 against Opus's 0.546 on the 38 tasks it was run on.

audio.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
audio.script: Today's pick from the AI Paper Digest. Teams of AI agents often look smarter than a lone model. But most tests compare them to a model answering once. That mixes up teamwork with simply spending more compute. The authors re-read earlier studies against baselines given the same budget. The advantage mostly vanished. In 74 percent of comparisons, the agents did no better, or worse. Talking only helps when agents see different evidence, use outside checks, or make different mistakes. Otherwise, sampling more may do just as well.
